claims.text: Williams published Algorithm 232, Heapsort, in Communications of the ACM volume 7 number 6 in June 1964, sorting an array of n records in place in time proportional to n log n.

source.title: Williams, J. W. J., Algorithm 232: Heapsort, Communications of the ACM 7(6):347-348, June 1964

claims.text: Floyd published Algorithm 245, Treesort 3, in Communications of the ACM volume 7 number 12 in December 1964, with the algorithm received in June and August of that year.

source.title: Floyd, R. W., Algorithm 245: Treesort 3, Communications of the ACM 7(12):701, December 1964

claims.text: Floyd’s contribution was an improvement to the construction phase, showing that a heap can be built from an unsorted array in linear time rather than the n log n that results from inserting the elements one at a time. This is the version most modern textbooks present as standard, and Floyd gave a complete, efficient implementation close to what is used today.

source.title: Floyd, R. W., Algorithm 245: Treesort 3, Communications of the ACM 7(12):701, December 1964

beats.broke: you need the smallest item repeatedly from a collection that keeps changing, and a full ordering is more than you need and too expensive to maintain
beats.fix: maintain only that each node is no larger than its children, which is exactly enough to know where the smallest is and cheap enough to restore after a change
beats.cost: the partial order tells you nothing about anything except the root, so the structure cannot be searched, iterated in order, or queried for second place
beats.interview: why building a heap from an array is linear when inserting n items one at a time is not
